title: Łuków’s Jewish Community: A Town Within a Town
summary: The book’s central subject is the community whose religious, social, political, and working life it records, and whose destruction gives the collection its urgency.
editorialContent:
![Łuków, the town where Jewish communal life took root](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/%C5%81uk%C3%B3w%2C_Kolegiata_Przemienienia_Pa%C5%84skiego%2C_21_V_2023_%283%29.jpg/1920px-%C5%81uk%C3%B3w%2C_Kolegiata_Przemienienia_Pa%C5%84skiego%2C_21_V_2023_%283%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## A community rooted in the town

The memorial book remembers Łuków’s Jews as a distinct community, with a history and institutions of their own, yet bound to the fortunes of the town around them. It calls them an old community of Podlasie and recalls Łuków’s place in a regional network that included [Międzyrzec](/communities/lukow/records/mention_c19363c97cebc261e9112db9), with which it sometimes disputed authority over nearby settlements. The book’s testimony places Jewish communal life within a wider [Polish setting](/communities/lukow/records/mention_7a520b4b56320af5bf661c6c), while local memory emphasizes the community’s own institutions, customs and political life.

The book’s historical introduction presents Łuków as one of the oldest Jewish settlements in Podlasie, but its different accounts do not supply a single, securely documented starting date. A modern overview likewise notes that accounts place Jewish settlement in the town as early as the mid-thirteenth century, while describing organized communal life from a later period. These early origins should therefore be treated as part of the town’s historical tradition, not as a precise founding date. ([History of the Jews in Łuków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_%C5%81uk%C3%B3w))

The community’s remembered identity was not simply religious. The book describes Jewish residents as industrious and relatively conservative, but such collective characterizations are the language of memoir, not a full portrait of every inhabitant. Its contributors also recall workers, traders, artisans, teachers, political activists and religious scholars. Their varied lives unfolded in [Łuków](/communities/lukow/records/mention_70c441b43b5a70c659e1d416), a town whose streets, markets and workshops were shared with non-Jewish neighbors.

## Synagogue, study and mutual responsibility

Religious institutions gave communal life its daily structure. The memorial book recalls the Great Synagogue, smaller prayer houses and study rooms, a yeshiva and a Talmud Torah. Among the institutions it names were the [Łuków synagogue](/communities/lukow/records/mention_f1e06ab8f3d0cc9f77771a62) and the [Talmud Torah](/communities/lukow/records/mention_ed7edbb615c430cf0eed0122), where poor children received religious education. The buildings and societies were not only places of worship: they connected generations, provided instruction and anchored mutual aid.

The book remembers Łuków as a center of Hasidic life, but it does not describe a community of one mind. Religious groups, political parties and generations differed over leadership and the future. Names preserved in the records make that communal world specific: [Meir Leib Gelernter](/communities/lukow/records/mention_cb9719e3489b567be00c6d31) is identified as an elected council member; other recollections name rabbis, communal leaders and activists. The memorial volume also remembers disputes involving the Agudah, whose representatives held substantial influence, and political groups that sought a different direction.

That civic and religious framework existed amid economic constraint. A contributor to the book describes Jewish Łuków as generally poor, with many people working in trade and crafts. Shoemakers, tailors and other workers served local customers and surrounding towns; some workshops and factories offered employment, though economic shocks could quickly undermine it. In its account of the early twentieth century, the book recalls the Bund’s organizing among workers and the growth of Zionist activity, alongside religious and Hasidic institutions. The result was not one “town within a town” with a single voice, but a dense, sometimes contentious community of overlapping associations and commitments.

## Belonging, boundaries and political change

The community’s relationship with the surrounding town was shaped both by interdependence and by unequal status. The memorial book recalls Jewish businesses and labor as part of Łuków’s economy, and describes neighbors whose livelihoods improved alongside the town’s commercial activity. At the same time, it recounts restrictions on Jewish communal authority and civic participation. The phrase “town within a town” captures this tension only if understood carefully: Jewish institutions created a strong communal world, but Jewish residents were not separate from the economic and political life of Łuków.

The book’s population figures also need to be read as snapshots from different periods, not as one continuous count. One record preserves a figure of 1,372 Jewish residents “at that time”; a later account gives quite different numbers for earlier and interwar years. A modern overview reports 6,145 Jews in 1921, while a memorial-book contributor gives 6,250. The discrepancy should remain visible rather than be resolved by choosing one number without evidence. In either account, Jewish residents formed a large part of the town’s population. ([History of the Jews in Łuków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_%C5%81uk%C3%B3w))

Political organization widened communal life beyond the synagogue and market. The memorial book recalls the Bund, Zionist currents, Agudah and other groups, with clubs, meetings, education and cultural activity. It also describes how emigration, war and economic hardship altered the community over time. A population count, then, can tell only part of the story: it cannot show the arguments at communal meetings, the work of a school, or the bonds formed in a study house.

## Occupation and destruction

German occupation turned communal boundaries into instruments of persecution. The memorial book records the establishment of the [Łuków ghetto](/communities/lukow/records/mention_76301e2ac4606782b1048c9c), the confinement of Jews in the town, and deportations to [Treblinka](/communities/lukow/records/mention_d0cc1f39b4d42e016c7b5345). Its testimony describes fear, deprivation and the breakdown of the institutions that had once organized daily life. The Jewish school, communal bodies and neighborhood networks were forced to operate under coercion and violence; people sought help and guidance from the Judenrat, an institution imposed within the machinery of occupation.

Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos independently documents Łuków as a ghetto site and records deportations and the movement of Jews through the region. Its account also notes that some families—many of them refugees—were transferred to Parczew before deportation to Treblinka. That detail underscores that Łuków’s wartime Jewish population included people driven from other places, not only longstanding residents. ([Yad Vashem, Łuków ghetto entry](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529))

The memorial book’s accounts and later summaries do not always give identical figures or describe each deportation in the same way. The broader history of the ghetto is often told through successive actions in autumn 1942 and its final liquidation in May 1943; the scale also reflects the arrival of Jews from neighboring towns and displaced communities. The Yad Vashem entry and the modern overview provide a wider regional frame, while the memorial book preserves how survivors remembered the destruction from within the community. ([Yad Vashem, Łuków ghetto entry](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529); [History of the Jews in Łuków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_%C5%81uk%C3%B3w))

Among the people remembered is Aaron Nota Freiberg, identified in the modern overview as the community’s last rabbi and reported murdered during the October 1942 deportations. That fate belongs to the history of the town’s destruction, but it does not encompass all its victims. The memorial book was assembled by survivors and former residents, and its record is necessarily partial: relatives who emigrated, died elsewhere or left no testimony may not appear in its narrative. Its account of the community’s end is therefore both indispensable and incomplete.

## What the memory preserves

The book calls Łuków’s prewar years a remarkable period of Jewish life, and remembers a community that had built institutions for worship, education, welfare, politics and culture. Independent records help set that memory against the larger history of German persecution and the destruction of Jewish life in the region. But the two kinds of evidence do different work: the archives establish historical context; the memorial book conveys what former residents chose to remember and the names through which they did so.

The title “a town within a town” should not obscure how closely Jewish and non-Jewish lives were intertwined. Łuków’s Jews built a richly organized communal world, but they also worked, traded and lived in the same town as their neighbors. The Holocaust destroyed that world through deliberate violence. Reading the community’s story means holding both truths together: its particularity, and its place in the shared history of Łuków.
